messages.subject: bug in lmer or in my head?
messages.subject_clean: bug in lmer or in my head?
messages.body_plain:
I'm teaching stats this semester and was trying to be all Barr-orthodox in my 
LME handout, so I played around with some fake data that I created somehow or 
other in 2008, originally designed for teaching minF'. But when trying to use 
likelihood ratio tests to test the significance of one factor, I got a bizarre 
result: in the reduced model, one of the factors was treated as if it had four 
levels in its interaction with the removed factor, when actually it has only 
two. The problem disappears if this factor is recoded by hand to a numerical 
variable using effect (sum) coding (-1 vs. 1).

I wasn't able to replicate this bizarre result in simpler data, so let me just 
show you using the original fake data set, which is here:

http://www.ccunix.ccu.edu.tw/~lngproc/doramiR.txt

This describes a fake experiment in which Dorami (who is, of course, the sister 
of Doraemon - no idea why all sorts of crap manga get translated into English, 
but not this classic - maybe because there's no blood or cheesecake) had a bunch 
of people with either a high school or college education respond (giving RTs) to 
a bunch of words: nouns and verbs, of high and low frequency (fully crossed). 
Every person gets words of all four types, so syntactic category and frequency 
are grouped by participant, and every item is responded to by people of both 
education levels, so education is grouped by item. (This is not a design 
addressed by Barr et al. 2013, since they're cognitive psychologists, not social 
or personality psychologists.)

Let's run the analysis, shall we?

# Load'er up

library(lme4) # I'm using R version 3.1.0, lme4 version 1.1-6, in Windows 7
ddat = read.delim("doramiR.txt")

# I purposely threw in some NA's, originally to show how
# by-participant and by-item means need not be the same

ddat = na.omit(ddat)

# Fixed factors still look pretty balanced

xtabs(~Education+SynCat+Freq, data=ddat)

# , , Freq = High
#
#             SynCat
# Education    Noun Verb
#   College      48   49
#   HighSchool   47   48
#
# , , Freq = Low
#
#             SynCat
# Education    Noun Verb
#   College      48   50
#   HighSchool   49   47

# I wanted the interactions to work as they do in ANOVA, rather than
# partially disappearing into the intercept as they do with R's default
# dummy (treatment) coding for factors, so I use effect (sum) coding
# - but this isn't responsible for the weird results, as further
# experiments showed (I leave this for the interested reader)

contrasts(ddat$Education) = contr.sum(levels(ddat$Education)) # 1 = College
contrasts(ddat$SynCat) = contr.sum(levels(ddat$SynCat)) # 1 = Noun
contrasts(ddat$Freq) = contr.sum(levels(ddat$Freq)) # 1 = High

# The maximal model, with fixed factors grouped as they should be,
# following Barr et al. (2013, p. 275): "In most cases, one should also have
# by-unit random slopes for any interactions where all factors comprising the
# interaction are within-unit; if any one factor involved in the interaction is
# between-unit, then the random slope associated with that interaction cannot
# be estimated, and is not needed."

ddat.lmer.max = lmer(RT~Education*SynCat*Freq # Fixed part
  +((SynCat*Freq)|Participant)+(Education|Item), data = ddat) # Random part
summary(ddat.lmer.max)

# Nothing but frequency is significant - I did that on purpose, because I'm
# kind of a jerk. The only weird thing in this summary are the super-high
# random correlations for SynCat and Freq, which I guess happen because
# I didn't create this fake data set with LME in mind. These correlations
# seem to be responsible for another curiosity, namely that the REML
# algorithm fails to converge when running a by-participants-only analysis,
# without the random Item factor (which I guess increases the proportion of
# the random "collinearity" enough to choke REML). I'm not sure, but I
# don't think this is relevant to the factor "bug"....

# Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
# Formula: RT ~ Education * SynCat * Freq + ((SynCat * Freq) | Participant) +
#     (Education | Item)
#    Data: ddat
#
# REML criterion at convergence: 5016.7
#
# Scaled residuals:
#     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max
# -1.8514 -0.6317 -0.2075  0.4085  3.9700
#
# Random effects:
#  Groups      Name          Variance Std.Dev. Corr
#  Participant (Intercept)     635.1   25.20
#              SynCat1         239.3   15.47    1.00
#              Freq1           185.0   13.60   -1.00 -0.99
#              SynCat1:Freq1  1095.8   33.10    0.05  0.13  0.03
#  Item        (Intercept)    1188.2   34.47
#              Education1      844.6   29.06   -0.33
#  Residual                  27146.5  164.76
# Number of obs: 386, groups: Participant, 20; Item, 20
#
# Fixed effects:
#                          Estimate Std. Error t value
# (Intercept)              742.9591    12.7177   58.42
# Education1                -0.4537    12.0234   -0.04
# SynCat1                   18.4146    11.9171    1.55
# Freq1                    -30.6700    11.8029   -2.60
# Education1:SynCat1         1.1824    11.1732    0.11
# Education1:Freq1          17.7279    11.0513    1.60
# SynCat1:Freq1              5.7752    13.5956    0.42
# Education1:SynCat1:Freq1  -3.0658    12.9484   -0.24
#
# Correlation of Fixed Effects:
#             (Intr) Edctn1 SynCt1 Freq1  Ed1:SC1 Ed1:F1 SC1:F1
# Education1  -0.114
# SynCat1      0.131  0.006
# Freq1       -0.112  0.000 -0.071
# Edctn1:SyC1  0.006  0.148 -0.131 -0.006
# Edctn1:Frq1  0.000 -0.126 -0.006 -0.134 -0.081
# SynCt1:Frq1  0.016 -0.005  0.023  0.007  0.000   0.006
# Edc1:SC1:F1 -0.005  0.017  0.000  0.005  0.026   0.007 -0.099

# Now I try to get a p value for Freq only, using a likelihood ratio test:
# I triple-checked this syntax in simpler cases, and I'm pretty sure it's right.

ddat.lmer.noFreq = lmer(RT~ (Education*SynCat)+(Education*SynCat):Freq
  +((SynCat*Freq)|Participant)+(Education|Item), data = ddat)

# But when running this, the chi-squared value is 0, since the two models
# are somehow considered to be identical:

anova(ddat.lmer.noFreq, ddat.lmer.max)

#                  Df    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)
# ddat.lmer.noFreq 22 5114.4 5201.5 -2535.2   5070.4
# ddat.lmer.max    22 5114.4 5201.5 -2535.2   5070.4     0      0  < 2.2e-16 ***

# Looking at the no-Freq results shows the problem:
# Education adds two extra levels in its interaction with Freq:
#  Education(-1) [implicit reference level]
#  Education1
#  EducationCollege
#  EducationHighSchool

summary(ddat.lmer.noFreq)

# Fixed effects:
#                           Estimate Std. Error t value
# (Intercept)               742.9591    12.7177   58.42
# Education1                 -0.4537    12.0234   -0.04
# SynCat1                    18.4146    11.9172    1.55
# Education1:SynCat1          1.1824    11.1732    0.11
# EducationCollege:Freq1    -12.9422    15.0472   -0.86
# EducationHighSchool:Freq1 -48.3979    17.2181   -2.81
# SynCat1:Freq1               5.7752    13.5956    0.42
# Education1:SynCat1:Freq1   -3.0658    12.9484   -0.24

# The problem is fixed by recoding Education by hand:

ddat$Education = 2*(ddat$Education=="College")-1

# Then start over again:

ddat.lmer.max.fix = lmer(RT~Education*SynCat*Freq
  +((SynCat*Freq)|Participant)+(Education|Item), data = ddat)
summary(ddat.lmer.max.fix)

# Same as before - so far so good

# Fixed effects:
#                         Estimate Std. Error t value
# (Intercept)             742.9591    12.7177   58.42
# Education                -0.4537    12.0234   -0.04
# SynCat1                  18.4146    11.9171    1.55
# Freq1                   -30.6700    11.8029   -2.60
# Education:SynCat1         1.1824    11.1732    0.11
# Education:Freq1          17.7279    11.0513    1.60
# SynCat1:Freq1             5.7752    13.5956    0.42
# Education:SynCat1:Freq1  -3.0658    12.9484   -0.24

# Recreate no-Freq model (same syntax as before):

ddat.lmer.noFreq.fix = lmer(RT~ (Education*SynCat)+(Education*SynCat):Freq
  +((SynCat*Freq)|Participant)+(Education|Item), data = ddat)

# No-Freq model looks OK now:

summary(ddat.lmer.noFreq.fix)

# Fixed effects:
#                         Estimate Std. Error t value
# (Intercept)             739.4937    14.2179   52.01
# Education                -0.4382    12.1119   -0.04
# SynCat1                  16.4284    13.5346    1.21
# Education:SynCat1         0.9499    11.2388    0.08
# Education:Freq1          13.9567    11.1204    1.26
# SynCat1:Freq1             6.0047    15.0334    0.40
# Education:SynCat1:Freq1  -2.9103    12.9739   -0.22

# Run likelihood ratio test

anova(ddat.lmer.noFreq.fix, ddat.lmer.max.fix)

#                Df    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)
# ddat.lmer.noFreq.fix 21 5119.3 5202.4 -2538.7 5077.3
# ddat.lmer.max.fix    22 5114.4 5201.5 -2535.2   5070.4 6.8956  1  0.008641 **

# That gives a p value close to what you get for the t = z method

nrow(ddat) # 386: Central Limit Theorem should help, if df relates mainly to n
2*pnorm(-2.60) # p = 0.009322376


So there you go - is the bug in lmer or in my head?

messages.body_plain:
Hey jm,

Well, you're not crazy. But it's not unique to lmer (the same thing happens
in plain lm), so it has something to do with the way contrasts are handled
with factors.  Note also that order matters: if you switch the relevant
part of the formula from (Education*SynCat):Freq to
(SynCat*Education):Freq, then you get the SynCat factor behaving in the
weird "split" way instead.  Same thing if you spell out each parameter
long-ways (i.e., without the * shorthand).  Why it should matter which one
comes first is beyond me.  Finally, the fact that you are setting contrasts
seems irrelevant, because if you leave it all as "treatment" coding, you
still get an analogous pattern.

So the issue, whatever it is, is not in your head, nor is it in lmer (or at
least, not uniquely) -- it's in the way factors (by which I mean the R data
class) are handled in the structure of the model.  It frankly gives me a
headache to try to interpret what all the coefficients actually mean in the
model without the "main effect" of Freq, but I can see why you're doing it
(as a practical workaround to get a p-value), and I think that makes sense
from that point of view.

I guess the moral of the story is that factors can have some unexpected
behavior (at least, unexpected to you or me) when you start dropping simple
effects but retain interactions.  Maybe this behavior makes sense
("feature" rather than "bug") to the authors, once you start thinking about
more general cases, like factors with many levels. But when you get down to
it, I think numeric coding of variables is the best way to exert absolute
control.

cheers,
-scott

where they have to rely on planned comparisons or post-hocs? - jm

> # EducationCollege:Freq1    -12.9422    15.0472   -0.86
> # EducationHighSchool:Freq1 -48.3979    17.2181   -2.81

> # Education1:SynCat1:Freq1   -3.0658    12.9484   -0.24

This isn't a bug in lmer, but rather a (extremely reasonable)
misunderstanding about how formulas work. Unfortunately most docs
don't try to explain the principles underlying formula interpretation
and just rely on people picking it up from examples...

The way to think about a formula like
  y ~ 1 + Education + SynCat + Education:SynCat
is that R *starts out* assuming dummy coding for everything. What that
formula means is that you want an intercept, and you want to allow the
predicted value of 'y' to be different for each level of Education,
and to be different for each level of SynCat, and to be different for
each combination of levels of Education & SynCat. (It may help to type
'Education:SynCat' at a regular prompt, not in a formula, and see what
you get.)

So that's the overall model we've asked R to fit. Now, as a second
step, R tries to figure out how to code it. If it just uses dummy
coding everywhere, then that will create a redundant
(overparametrized) model, which would be a bit annoying. In
particular, that Education:SynCat term encompasses *all* of the other
terms, so we could drop any subset of the other terms from our formula
and R would still fit the same overall model. So R doesn't use those
terms to decide what model to fit, it just uses them to decide what
parametrization to use. The way this works is, R goes through from
left to right (after sorting low-order interactions before high-order
interactions), and for each term it asks "do I need to switch any of
these factors from dummy coding to contrast coding in order to avoid
redundancy with the stuff to its left?"

In this case, the answer is yes, every factor in every term needs to
use contrast coding, so that's what R does. This is why a formula like
"~ Education" (which is implicitly expanded to "~ 1 + Education")
gives you contrast coding, but a formula like "~ 0 + Education" gives
you dummy coding. And the same logic explains how R interprets other
formulas like "~ 1 + Education + Education:SynCat" or "~ 0 + Education
+ Education:SynCat" or "~ 0 + Education:SynCat" -- these all give "the
same model" in the sense that they all create design matrices with the
same column space, but they encode it differently. (However, if you
try "~1 + Education:SynCat" you actually will get an overparametrized
model, because R is buggy!)

The fixed effect part second model expands to

~ 1 + Education + SynCat + Education:SynCat + Education:Freq +
SynCat:Freq + Education:SynCat:Freq

notice that the 1 + Education + Education:Freq part of this is exactly
like one of the smaller models I used as an example above. R notices
that you want all combinations of Education:Freq to affect the result,
and since Freq does not otherwise appear in the model, the only way to
accomplish this is to use dummy coding for Education.

I can't off the top of my head think of a better way to fit the
restricted model you were trying to fit than to escape R's coding
system entirely by coding it by hand, as you did. I don't really think
this should be considered a flaw in R's coding system, though, because
the model you want to fit violates the principle of marginality and
AFAICT makes no sense (in that it imposes a complicated and
implausible constraint on the fitted model -- your final "by-hand"
model isn't testing for a main effect or an interaction, it's testing
some sort of weird constraint that I can't even figure out and that
depends on the details of your coding scheme, like "does Freq matter
for this specific combination of Education and SynCat but not this
other one" -- something like that). Generally if you want to check for
whether Freq matters, you should compare to a model where Freq has
been removed entirely, and only check for main effects after first
removing interactions (this is the "principle of marginality").

--

can't muster the self-control to avoid chipping in another two cents, sorry:

I also agree with you that the smaller model "makes no sense," in the sense
that I have a helluva time wrapping my head around the interpretation of

its own.  However, the "main effect" (since it's coded with sum coding) of
Freq in the full model is the parameter of interest in the full model, and
it makes sense to want to test the hypothesis that, in the context of the
full model, there is an overall significant effect of the Freq manipulation
(or more precisely, see if one can reject the null hypothesis that there is
no effect).  And this is distinct from removing Freq entirely from the
model, which would be testing the hypothesis that Freq doesn't matter at
all.

But I think JM's purpose here is to use a model-comparison LRT for testing
this hypothesis, basically to get around the "problem of no p-value" for
the original estimate.  I don't see any problems with this per se, though
it does hint at the overall lack of a standard approach to hypothesis
testing in NHST when lmer doesn't give p-values.  I mean, the original
effect had a t of -2.6, which is very clearly significant at p < .05.  But
if an analyst would like to get a more precise p-value without having to
choose among the various options for computing df's for this kind of model,
and do so in a way that can be applied to other arbitrary hypothesis tests
in a consistent way (i.e., using LRT's for *all* tests of interest), then I
think this kind of model comparison makes sense.

But yeah, I agree that the model itself is kinda wonky, taken as-is, and
R's under-the-hood dummy-coding isn't inherently flawed by taking this
approach to specification.  Basically R has to do a little mind-reading
with the dummy-coding, but this doesn't work for every case, like this one.

> This isn't a bug in lmer, but rather a (extremely reasonable)

> The way to think about a formula like

> formula means is that you want an intercept, and you want to allow the
> predicted value of 'y' to be different for each level of Education,

> (or more precisely, see if one can reject the null hypothesis that there is
> no effect).  And this is distinct from removing Freq entirely from the

What is the difference between testing whether the "Freq manipulation"
has an effect, and testing whether "Freq doesn't matter at all"?

This isn't just an issue of the particular details of this model, it's
a fundamental problem that main effects simply cannot be interpreted
as being "main" when there are also interactions present. Including
Education:Freq and SynCat:Freq means that you are assuming that the
effect of Freq can vary depending on the levels of Education and
SynCat. It doesn't make much sense to assume that Freq's effect can
vary while simultaneously testing the hypothesis that it has no
effect.

I think in practice you end up testing some hypothesis that looks
like: "if I calculate the Freq effect for each subgroup of my
population (as defined by combinations of the other factors), and then
take some weighted average of these different frequency effects, then
I test whether that weighted average is zero". And the weights depend
in a complicated way on what coding system is used, how many data
points you have in each cell, etc. Like you might turn out to be
testing whether the sum of the Freq effects in the
Education=HighSchool:SynCat=Noun group and the
Education=College:SynCat=Verb group is equal to 0.73 times the Freq
effect in the Education=HighSchool:SynCat=Verb group, or something
like that.
These are very very rarely the kinds of hypotheses that you actually
want to test.

--

Well, I think it's just analogous to testing a main effect in an ANOVA that
also has interactions specified.  The way people treat interpretation of
ANOVAs is that they look at interactions, and if those are not significant,
you interpret the main effects.  If interactions are significant, then
interpretation of main effects is tricky at best, but mostly incoherent, or
at least opaque, as you point out (and I agree!).  But I think the "main
effect" parameter in the full model has a pretty clear interpretation,
which is just the marginal effect estimate collapsing across the
interactions, etc.  I'm on the side of the fence that believes if you have
enough data, you should be fitting as complex a model as makes sense, and
interpreting from there.  For example, in this case, one of the interaction
terms is marginal (i.e., big-ish, but not "significant").  Removing too
many of these can get you pretty biased results, and I'd put more stock in
the "main effect" estimate that takes these into account rather than an
estimate from a model that drops all the interactions because they don't
hit p < .05.  Of course, overfitting is something to watch out for, too,
but blind model-selection by p-value is rarely a great idea.  It's the same
principle for leaving in regression coefficients in a plain multiple
regression, even if those coefs don't hit p < .05, because overall that
model should provide better estimates of the effects that you are
interested in.

So if the goal is to get the best estimates for any given effect, sticking
with the biggest model possible makes sense (with the caveat of possible
overfitting).  JM's problem (I'm guessing) is just that he'd like to get a
p-value for that estimate of the marginal effect of Freq across various
(potential) interactions.  I think his model-comparison LRT approach is as
good as any other, where alternative methods are to use a t > 2 == p < .05
rule of thumb, or to pick one of the methods for estimating a df for the
t-test on the parameter (like SAS/SPSS/etc. do).

Or am I missing something?  I do see your point about the need to think
about what the marginal estimate is marginal over, especially with
unbalanced data.  JM's data was still relatively balanced.  But I think
this is only really a problem if he wanted to actually interpret the coefs
in the weird subset model, which I do not think is the case.

But if I'm missing something, I'd be happy to hear it.

Hi James,

like others have said, this is by design of how R treats formulas. I had this exact questions some time ago and asked on SO on how to avoid this: http://stackoverflow.com/q/11335923/289572

Out of this discussion I developed the mixed function in the afex package which circumvents this problem by manually altering the model matrix. This function gives you the p-values right away and replicates your results (with one caveat described below).

require(afex)

ddat = read.delim("http://www.ccunix.ccu.edu.tw/~lngproc/doramiR.txt")
ddat = na.omit(ddat)
contrasts(ddat$Education) = contr.sum(levels(ddat$Education)) # 1 = College
contrasts(ddat$SynCat) = contr.sum(levels(ddat$SynCat)) # 1 = Noun
contrasts(ddat$Freq) = contr.sum(levels(ddat$Freq)) # 1 = High

m1 <- mixed(RT~Education*SynCat*Freq+((SynCat*Freq)|Participant)+(Education|Item), data = ddat, method = "LRT", check.contrasts=FALSE)
m1

##                  Effect df.large df.small chisq df p.value

On Thu, May 8, 2014 at 2:34 PM, Scott Jackson <scottuba-Re5JQEeQqe8AvxtiuMwx3w at public.gmane.org> wrote:
> Well, I think it's just analogous to testing a main effect in an ANOVA that
> also has interactions specified.  The way people treat interpretation of
> ANOVAs is that they look at interactions, and if those are not significant,
> you interpret the main effects.  If interactions are significant, then
> interpretation of main effects is tricky at best, but mostly incoherent, or
> at least opaque, as you point out (and I agree!).  But I think the "main
> effect" parameter in the full model has a pretty clear interpretation, which
> is just the marginal effect estimate collapsing across the interactions,
> etc.

Having reviewed a bit, right, if you're careful (choosing the right
coding scheme etc.) then you can set up your design matrix in such a
way that the "main effect" parameter is estimating some well-defined
quantity. But I'm still pretty skeptical that this particular quantity
will be of scientific interest. In particular, it usually cannot be
generalized to make predictions about even closely related
experimental designs, because when you marginalize out the other
effects, you assume some particular distribution over them. Knowing
the marginal effect of Freq in a population with this particular mix
of education levels, syntactic type exposures, etc., doesn't tell you
anything about the effect of Freq in any particular person, or even
about the marginal effect in other populations where these quantities
are differently distributed.

> I'm on the side of the fence that believes if you have enough data,
> you should be fitting as complex a model as makes sense, and interpreting
> from there.  For example, in this case, one of the interaction terms is
> marginal (i.e., big-ish, but not "significant").  Removing too many of these
> can get you pretty biased results, and I'd put more stock in the "main
> effect" estimate that takes these into account rather than an estimate from
> a model that drops all the interactions because they don't hit p < .05.  Of
> course, overfitting is something to watch out for, too, but blind
> model-selection by p-value is rarely a great idea.  It's the same principle
> for leaving in regression coefficients in a plain multiple regression, even
> if those coefs don't hit p < .05, because overall that model should provide
> better estimates of the effects that you are interested in.
>
> So if the goal is to get the best estimates for any given effect, sticking
> with the biggest model possible makes sense (with the caveat of possible
> overfitting).

Yes, definitely. I usually compare the full model to the one where the
factor doesn't appear at all ("does this factor matter at all?"), and
to the model that only has a main effect ("does this factor interact
with other factors?"). Those are both tests against the full model, so
we never have to "accept the null" by throwing out non-significant
terms, and AFAICT they are sensible ways to test the main questions
that psychologists usually care about.

> JM's problem (I'm guessing) is just that he'd like to get a
> p-value for that estimate of the marginal effect of Freq across various
> (potential) interactions.

I just think that *really* wanting such a thing is sufficiently
unusual that if you do want it, you should have a clear, articulable
reason for why.

That said, and to answer one of the original questions in the thread
-- if you really do want this, then the Anova function in the 'car'
package is documented to work on lme4 models, and accepts a type="III"
argument, so this might be the simplest and most elegant way to do
this strange thing ;-).

-n

--

>> This isn't a bug in lmer, but rather a (extremely reasonable)
>> misunderstanding about how formulas work. Unfortunately most docs
>> don't try to explain the principles underlying formula interpretation
>> and just rely on people picking it up from examples...
>> 
>> The way to think about a formula like
>>  y ~ 1 + Education + SynCat + Education:SynCat
>> is that R *starts out* assuming dummy coding for everything. What that
>> formula means is that you want an intercept, and you want to allow the
>> predicted value of 'y' to be different for each level of Education,
>> and to be different for each level of SynCat, and to be different for
>> each combination of levels of Education & SynCat. (It may help to type
>> 'Education:SynCat' at a regular prompt, not in a formula, and see what
>> you get.)
>> 
>> So that's the overall model we've asked R to fit. Now, as a second
>> step, R tries to figure out how to code it. If it just uses dummy
>> coding everywhere, then that will create a redundant
>> (overparametrized) model, which would be a bit annoying. In
>> particular, that Education:SynCat term encompasses *all* of the other
>> terms, so we could drop any subset of the other terms from our formula
>> and R would still fit the same overall model. So R doesn't use those
>> terms to decide what model to fit, it just uses them to decide what
>> parametrization to use. The way this works is, R goes through from
>> left to right (after sorting low-order interactions before high-order
>> interactions), and for each term it asks "do I need to switch any of
>> these factors from dummy coding to contrast coding in order to avoid
>> redundancy with the stuff to its left?"
>> 
>> In this case, the answer is yes, every factor in every term needs to
>> use contrast coding, so that's what R does. This is why a formula like
>> "~ Education" (which is implicitly expanded to "~ 1 + Education")
>> gives you contrast coding, but a formula like "~ 0 + Education" gives
>> you dummy coding. And the same logic explains how R interprets other
>> formulas like "~ 1 + Education + Education:SynCat" or "~ 0 + Education
>> + Education:SynCat" or "~ 0 + Education:SynCat" -- these all give "the
>> same model" in the sense that they all create design matrices with the
>> same column space, but they encode it differently. (However, if you
>> try "~1 + Education:SynCat" you actually will get an overparametrized

>>

>> accomplish this is to use dummy coding for Education.

>> been removed entirely, and only check for main effects after first
>> removing interactions (this is the "principle of marginality").

Hi all

I have a doctoral student who is working with ordinal data (acceptability judgements from employers of migrant workers' pronunciation) with ordinal predictors (9-point ratings of various pronunciation features). He's been using clmm for the ordinal DV, but we're having difficulty getting stable models because of multicollinearity between the predictors (at least, that is what we think the problem is - the warning is of rank deficiency, resulting in clmm dropping one or more coefficient from the model). I've suggested centering the predictors (e.g. using Florian Jaeger's myCenter() ), but my concern is that this turns ordinal into numeric. I'm not sure how big a concern this is, given that the ratings are on a linear scale of 1-9, but I have read some fairly strong warnings about ordinal vs numeric (e.g. pj.freefaculty.org/Papers/MidWest09/Midwest09.pdf).

Does anyone have advice around building models with ordinal DVs and ordinal predictors?

Paul

I don't know how much data you have, but trying to separately estimate
the effect of each and every possible rating for each possible value
of each different rating does seem like a lot to ask of a typical
psycholinguistic data set. (Do you even have observations at every
value of all the rating scales? If not then that'll be your
collinearity problem right there...)

Treating ordinal variables as numeric *per se* isn't problematic --
the problem discussed in that paper is about what happens if you treat
ordinal variables as *linear* (i.e., assuming that on your scale the
difference between 1 and 2 is the same as the difference between 4 and
5 or 8 and 9.). But it might make sense to treat it as numeric but
with possible non-linearities -- e.g. treating it as numeric with a
9th order polynomial model or a 9 dof spline basis will give identical
results as if you treat it as ordinal. But non-linear models also give
you the option of using, say, 3 degrees of freedom, which is probably
enough to capture the broad shape of whatever non-linearities are in
your rating scale, but still allow for pooling data between similar
observations.

Normally I'd suggest using mgcv here, but I don't know that it has any
support for ordinal DVs. A simple workaround that might work okay
would be to use the standard R 'bs' function (in the 'splines'
library), something like 'y ~ bs(my_ordinal_as_numeric, dof)', where
'dof' is a number between 1 and 8.

the data come from an on-line Qualtrics survey in which employers heard speech samples from migrants and rated them on 9-point scales for 'acceptability for employment' (the DV of interest) as well as on 9-point pronunciation scales such as 'intonation', 'lexical stress', etc., and the aim now is to determine the extent to which the pronunciation ratings are good predictors of the 'acceptability' rating. There are also expert ratings of pronunciation features from experienced ESOL teachers that will be used in a separate analysis (again with the 'acceptability' rating as the DV).
The speech data come from 40 speakers, and there were 95 employers who carried out the ratings, but in 2 groups - all groups rated for 'acceptabilty' but one group rated for the pronunciation features while the other rated  'attitudinal' type features like 'friendliness'. The two groups are being treated separately for this initial analysis. As the task is very time consuming, each employer only rated a subset of the speakers in their group, with selection designed to ensure as even a distribution as possible.
Employer and Speaker are treated as random effects.

hope that helps
Paul

In my experience, this is more important than (say) the number of ordinal categories when analyzing as if it were continuous.  And what are the ordinal predictors like?  Is this an experimental design with ordinal factors, or an observational/pseudo-experimental design with a bunch of variables?  What do the predictor distributions looks like?


On Mon, May 19, 2014 at 10:18 PM, Paul Warren <Paul.Warren-O5iVTVtUEt6lVyrhU4qvOw at public.gmane.org<mailto:Paul.Warren-O5iVTVtUEt6lVyrhU4qvOw at public.gmane.org>> wrote:
Hi all

I have a doctoral student who is working with ordinal data (acceptability judgements from employers of migrant workers' pronunciation) with ordinal predictors (9-point ratings of various pronunciation features). He's been using clmm for the ordinal DV, but we're having difficulty getting stable models because of multicollinearity between the predictors (at least, that is what we think the problem is - the warning is of rank deficiency, resulting in clmm dropping one or more coefficient from the model). I've suggested centering the predictors (e.g. using Florian Jaeger's myCenter() ), but my concern is that this turns ordinal into numeric. I'm not sure how big a concern this is, given that the ratings are on a linear scale of 1-9, but I have read some fairly strong warnings about ordinal vs numeric (e.g. pj.freefaculty.org/Papers/MidWest09/Midwest09.pdf<http://pj.freefaculty.org/Papers/MidWest09/Midwest09.pdf>).

Does anyone have advice around building models with ordinal DVs and ordinal predictors?

Paul

Here are my thoughts, hope they help.

- First, plot your data.  Look at lots and lots of plots.  Histograms with
binwidth = 1 should give you nice charts for each variable (DV and
predictors) that give you a sense of distributions.  It may be that some
values of the scales are never used, or used incredibly rarely (like twice
or something), and that could cause problems for the clmm.  At least in the
DV.  Weird distributions in the predictors may end up making interpretation
harder, but shouldn't really impact the model's ability to reach a fit.
- Look at bivariate plots by using jitter or a heatmap or something,
because otherwise overplotting will obscure anything interesting.
- I'm recommending lots and lots of plots because I'm assuming this is a
new type of data collection (i.e., you haven't been using this instrument
for a long time), and it may be that there are some weird things going on
that you should find out about, before you even worry about fitting models.
- If you're going to center (which is nearly always a good idea), I would
actually recommend centering at value 5 (the middle of your scale) rather
than the empirical mean.  There's nothing special about mean-centering
that's so much better for fitting purposes compared to this, and centering
to the middle of your scale will make things easier to interpret (I think),
especially if your middle value has some kind of meaningful label.
- Double-check how you're splitting the data for analysis based on the two
Employer groups.  For example, use something like droplevels() to make sure
that when you analyze one group, it's only estimating the random effects of
Employer that are in that one group, as opposed to all of the levels of
Employer.
- It sounds like the design is basically a planned missing data design.
 How many people did each Employer rate?  This might end up being the main
culprit for the rank deficiency, depending on how much data ended up in
each combination of speakers and employers, etc.  Ultimately you may want
to consider a more thorough method for handling the missingness.  Multiple
imputation is the "gold standard", at least in my experience.  The "mice"
package is one of the better ones, and the documentation is pretty good,
especially if you track down his papers on it.  If you go this route and
run into trouble at the "pooling" step (that is, pooling results across the
imputations), let me know, I may have some code that can help.  But there
may also be a reasonable version of hot-decking or other type of single
imputation that will get you good results.  It might be worth it to try a
simple imputation method first, just to see if this helps address the rank
deficiency issue, before you worry too much about the most appropriate
imputation method.  A simple "hotdeck" just fills in a missing value with a
value that's drawn from the observed responses.  So if Employer 5 didn't
rate Speaker 6, then you fill in those values by pulling randomly from the
values that were observed for Speaker 6 (i.e., from the other Employers).
 This is miles better than mean replacement (for one, it preserves the
overall distribution of responses compared to the observed distribution),
and may help with the rank deficiency.  But it's probably not the best
final solution for the analysis.  Just something to try as an initial step.
- I don't think there's a problem with treating the predictors as numeric
per se, but the plotting may reveal some things that make you re-think how
to represent them.  In general, for any kind of regression, there are no
real distributional assumptions about the predictors.  So as long as a "one
unit change" on a predictor seems meaningful (which you may re-evaluate
after seeing the plots), then I don't see a problem treating the predictors
as numerical.  That paper you linked to gives a nice example of when this
isn't the case, namely that the scale is really better understood as a
scale of political extremity rather than a scale of "Republican-ness".
 This may also be the case with some of your scales, but maybe not all of
them.  Looking at lots of plots and thinking very hard are really your best
tools here, and I think will be better than trying to sort out the results
of a complicated fitted model with a jillion dummy-coded categorical
predictors.
- For collinearity issues, it may end up being best to just combine some
scales.  This is common in lots of different kinds of measurement
instruments, where groups of items represent multiple indicators or facets
of some underlying scale or factors.  You may have in fact designed the
items in this way, either on purpose or by accident.  I mean, if you have a
lot of "attitudinal" items, then maybe these could be grouped in some way,
like 5 items that deal with work attitudes, 5 items that deal with social
attitudes, or whatever.  And if you end up combining items that also end up
highly related empirically, then that should help with the worst of the
collinearity.

Hope that helps, and good luck!  It sounds like a very rich data set, so I
would highly recommend exploring it carefully with lots of visualization
before jumping ahead prematurely to hypothesis-testing.
-scott
